findings.text: The first paragraph tells a newcomer what Athena is, who it is for and what problem it solves. It answers both "what is it" and "why it matters" in a few sentences.
findings.source: Header lede: "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository... It solves the problem of AI edits that arrive unreviewed and unaccountable."

findings.text: The page is Athena's home URL, but its title and almost all of its body are about a different project (firstmate). A newcomer looking for Athena has to work out from the second lede paragraph that they are reading a sample of Athena's output, not documentation for Athena.
findings.source: Page title and h1: "Athena explains how firstmate handles work"

findings.text: The first section after the header is a visible failure message. It shows none of the models, verdict or cost that the lede promises Athena records, so the newcomer's first look at proof is an error.
findings.source: Check it on a real job: "The records of job 20261029-073603-7kqv could not be read here, so no models, verdict or costs are shown: no reading record for job 20261029-073603-7kqv."

findings.text: This link is aimed at the site owner, not a newcomer, and it appears beside the main next-step link without explanation. It may confuse first-time readers.
findings.source: Header: "Owner view: proposals waiting for your decision."

findings.text: The next step is concrete: prerequisites, clone, `./setup.sh`, and a one-line example command. The header links straight to it, so "what do I do next" is answered well.
findings.source: Next steps: "Before installing, have git 2.40 or later, a C linker, curl, and either Claude Code or npm" ... "athena ask \"add a changelog\""

findings.text: The firstmate study is careful and readable at its top level. It defines terms before using them and gives a plain start-to-finish walkthrough, which helps a newcomer judge the quality of Athena's output.
findings.source: Start here: "Firstmate is a tool that keeps a backlog of programming tasks and hands each one to a separate AI coding tool, called a worker"

findings.text: The States and Counters lists give only a name, a tag and claim ids (for example "places-held, changed by transitions t1, t3, t4, t9, t11"). A newcomer gets little from these lists, and they add to the page's length and density.
findings.source: States of a piece of work: "Read each line as the state's name, its kind, and the claims that support it."

findings.text: This closing note refers to the internal repository layout, which means nothing to a first-time visitor.
findings.source: About this page: "is the name of the folder under studies/ that holds the data this page is generated from."
